entries.title: Manual Cinema’s Christmas Carol
entries.summary: <p>Manual Cinema’s awe-inspiring, one-of-a-kind rendition of the Dickens classic returns to the Studebaker Theater this holiday season! </p><p>Avowed holiday skeptic Aunt Trudy has been reluctantly recruited to carry on her late husband Joe’s tradition of spreading Christmas cheer. Alone in her Chicago home on Christmas Eve, she reconstructs his annual Christmas Carol puppet show over a Zoom call, while the family celebrates from afar. But as Trudy dives deeper into the story, the puppets take on a life of their own and the family call transforms into a breathtaking, one-of-a-kind cinematic reimagining of Dickens’s classic ghost story. </p><p>Featuring hundreds of handmade puppets, immersive sound design and live music, <b>Manual Cinema’s <i>Christmas Carol</i></b> is a holiday show unlike anything you’ve ever seen. <a class="Link" href="https://fineartsbuilding.com/events/christmas-carol" target="_blank" >Get tickets!</a></p><p>“Extraordinarily moving”<br>– Chris Jones, <i>Chicago Tribune</i></p><p>“Unlike anything I’ve ever seen”<br>– <i>Chicago On Stage</i></p><p>“Simply hypnotic”<br>– <i>Chicago Reader</i></p><p>“Immersive and captivating”<br>– <i>Newcity Stage</i></p>

entries.title: Bears DT Jeffery Simmons embraces 'the moment' with 3 sacks in a 21-13 win over Saints
entries.summary: <p>When <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> needed it most Sunday, when it was absolutely necessary that someone step up and make a big play, defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons was exactly the man to make it happen.</p><p>The Saints were still threatening for a comeback in the final two minutes as quarterback Tyler Shough lined up for a snap just outside the red zone, and the only thought in Simmons’ mind was, “Go win the game.”</p><p>He knew the best way to do it. Before the snap, he told defensive end Austin Booker to switch spots with him, shifting Simmons to the outside and a one-on-one matchup with rookie right tackle Mason Murphy.</p><p>It went just like Simmons expected.</p><p>He blew through Murphy with a swim move, got his hands around Shough’s waist and whirled him around for his third sack. The Saints settled for a field goal a few plays later and ran out of gas as the Bears held on for a 21-13 win.</p><p>“It’s just being in the moment, owning that moment and winning that moment,” Simmons said. “The plays will come to you. When it really matters, this team brought me here and they expect me to win, especially in my one-on-ones, so I take full advantage of them.”</p><p>The Bears didn’t have someone like this a month ago. They had good players on defense, but nobody who could take the game into his own hands like Simmons.</p><p>And Simmons, playing for the aimless, anonymous Titans, didn’t have a stage like this until the Bears traded for him.</p><p>The three sacks matched his career high and was the most by a Bears defensive tackle since Jeremiah Ratliff in 2014. With five in his first three games, Simmons is now tied with Booker for the team lead and has eclipsed the four sacks he had in seven games with the Titans. He’s two away from matching his single-season best of 11.</p><p>The Bears also got a sack for a safety by Montez Sweat and one sack each from defensive backs Cam Lewis and Clark Phillips for a total of six, their most in a game since 2021.</p><p>“It’s a race: Who can get there first?” Sweat said. “[Simmons] was getting there a little faster than some other people. It was a great one for him and the whole d-line.</p><p>“We faced a lot of scrutiny coming into this season. We heard that. We’re answering the bell.”</p><p>As the offense struggled to bury the Saints, the defense stepped up at every turn to maintain margin.</p><p>Rookie safety Dillon Thieneman came up big in the second quarter when he sniffed out a reverse and dropped wide receiver Barion Brown for a loss, then two plays later picked up standout wide receiver Chris Olave in coverage and intercepted Shough’s pass. That set up a touchdown to put the Bears ahead 16-0.</p><p>The Bears went up 21-10 on Sweat’s first career safety with 12:55 left on a play in which Simmons was on the sideline.</p><p>With five minutes left, the Saints were down 11 and scrambling. Simmons’ late sack for a 13-yard loss stuck them in second-and-23, all but forcing them to kick a field goal and try an onside kick. Luther Burden clamped down on it, and it was all kneel-downs from there.</p><p>“When it really matters, guys have to make plays, and that’s what we did across the board,” Simmons said.</p><p>It was a group effort, as he said, in making it a miserable day for the Saints’ offense and Shough, who finished with a 71.7 passer rating, but Simmons was at the heart of it. As rare as it is to acquire a player of his ability in the middle of the season, it’s rarer still for that player to walk in and take charge from the start.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/05/new-bears-dt-jeffery-simmons-arrival-at-halas-hall-has-been-flawless-on-and-off-the-field" >Simmons became a pseudo-captain the moment he walked in the door at Halas Hall</a>. He’s gigantic. He’s a relentless worker who tries to light that same fire under everyone around him. And he’s excellent.</p><p>All of that makes him easy to follow.</p><p>“He's quickly becoming a voice that everyone hears and everyone rallies behind,” coach Ben Johnson said.</p><p>Quarterback Caleb Williams called Simmons “a momentum changer,” he certainly was in a game in which Williams managed just 181 yards passing, the rushing attack was stilted and the Bears scored just once — a field goal — in their final six possessions.</p><p>Simmons said he always has played like this, with passion and a will to dominate, but since getting traded to a contender in a big market, “You guys are actually getting a chance to see it now.”</p><p>He’s also getting more pass-rushing opportunities on a Bears team that hasn’t trailed for one second during his time with them than he saw on a Titans team that was 1-6 when it dealt him.</p><p>Simmons is right that he always has been a monster. He’s spent most of his career getting double-teamed and still managed to make four Pro Bowls, plus an All-Pro selection last season. He really isn’t doing anything different.</p><p>What’s different is that it matters more here. He’s no longer making plays for a plunging team that’s irrelevant in the national landscape. He’s in the thick of a playoff race in a city starved for star power on that side of the ball. That’s the moment he’s embracing.</p>

entries.title: Lewandowski scores, but Fire drop playoff opener against Charlotte
entries.summary: <p>Pep Biel scored off a rebound of his penalty kick in the 11th minute of stoppage time after a hand-ball foul on Jack Elliot, and Charlotte FC beat the Fire 2-1 on Sunday at SeatGeek Stadium in Bridgeview for the first regulation playoff victory in club history.</p><p>Josh Cohen replaced starting goalkeeper Chris Brady late in stoppage time with a penalty shootout on the horizon and surrendered the winner. Biel's goal was his first in his third postseason appearance.</p><p>Liel Abada put an end to a scoreless match three minutes into the second half when he used assists from defender Henry Kessler and Ashley Westwood to score with a header off a set piece for his first goal in his sixth postseason appearance.</p><p>Kessler collected his first assist in his first playoff match with the club after not contributing to a goal in six postseason matches with the New England Revolution. Westwood's assist was his first in his eighth playoff appearance with Charlotte.</p><p>Robert Lewandowski used his head to score the equalizer in the 68th minute for the Fire in his first postseason appearance. Defender Jonathan Dean notched his second assist in four playoff matches and Philip Zinckernagel picked up his third in three postseason outings.</p><p>Kristijan Kahlina saved four shots for No. 5 seed Charlotte (16-10-9).</p><p>Brady finished with two saves and Cohen had one for fourth-seeded Chicago (16-12-7).</p><p>The Fire swept the regular-season series with a 2-1 victory at home to start August and a 1-0 victory on the road to close out September.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>The Fire travel to Charlotte for the middle match on Saturday.</p>

entries.title: Davis Martin talks trade from White Sox, shin injury
entries.summary: <p>The night that the most enjoyable season of his career ended in Cleveland last month, Davis Martin was commiserating with other White Sox pitchers when Erick Fedde made a comment he’s been thinking about more recently.</p><p>“He said ‘This team will never be the same,’” Martin recalled in a phone interview with the Sun-Times.</p><p>Turnover is constant in baseball, but the quote hit home on Thursday, when Martin was having ice cream with family and saw a call coming from White Sox general manager Chris Getz.</p><p>The longest-tenured White Sox player until he was traded to the Colorado Rockies last week alongside Luis Castillo in exchange for two prospects, Martin said the conversation with Getz was filled with appreciative comments in both directions. It was immediately followed by a litany of calls from Rockies front office members, and the deal reunites Martin with former White Sox pitching coach Ethan Katz, just hired into the same role with Colorado.</p><p>This was the first offseason of Martin’s career where he thought change was possible, but the news still was “a shock,” wholly removed from the salary shedding mechanics that brought it into reality. By Sunday, Martin was still working to respond to every coach, every sports psychologist, every security guard that reached out about the move.</p><p>“Shows you how long I've been there,” Martin said. “It's hard not to reminisce and think about how fast not only eight years went, but all the stuff that happened in those eight years. Having a kid, getting married, all that. A lot of life events happened while I was a Chicago White Sox. We just let ourselves sit in it, and it was heavy.”</p><p>After enduring a 121-loss 2024 season, the affable and upbeat Martin easily summons optimism about pitching in Denver’s hitter-friendly Coors Field, or hope about the rebuilding Rockies’ young core. After ‘24, Martin had family members ask if he wanted a trade to a better organization, and he’d retort that he would rather be part of a once-unfathomable White Sox turnaround instead.</p><p>This September in the visitor’s clubhouse of Kauffman Stadium, the same ballpark where he made his 2022 major-league debut, Martin celebrated that turnaround as the Sox clinched their first playoff berth of his tenure. Martin’s wife Jenna kept on him to be present, and treasure every moment of the 2026 season, and it wasn’t hard to catch glimpses of Martin in that champagne-soaked scrum looking around, taking it all in.</p><p>“It was very special,” Martin said. “A little picturesque, storybook ending.”</p><p>A suggested edit to the storybook might be for Martin to have ended it healthy. A sensational first two months showcased “a ceiling I maybe didn’t even know was there” to his game, but Martin battled a stress reaction in his right shin throughout the season. The 29-year-old said the issue would’ve required 2-3 months of rest to fully subside, so he managed as best he could, to diminishing returns down the stretch.</p><p>“Waking up at two or three in the morning after starts, and your whole leg is throbbing, can't go back to sleep, and hobbling around and trying to piece together your lower half before every outing,” Martin said, serving to explain why he understood his minimal role in the postseason. “I want to win the game more than I care about my own statistics.”</p><p>For Martin, the prospect of full health fuels optimism that he can lead another turnaround in Colorado, and look more like his first-half of 2026 while doing it. Whether the Sox would be seeking to upgrade their rotation without him if his leg held up all year long, will remain a hypothetical.</p><p>To sum up his feelings, Martin naturally opted to paraphrase Jordan Davis, a now-former member of his beloved Philadelphia Eagles, about being traded away from a place he still loves.</p><p>“Even if I'm getting sent away, if it helps them in any way in the future, I'm happy, and that’s kind of how I felt,” Martin said. “It's a special team, a special organization to me, and it always will be.”</p>

entries.title: Bulls veteran Norman Powell will be sidelined with a tweaked hamstring
entries.summary: <p>The next-guy-up moments continued for the Bulls on Sunday.</p><p>Already losing prized rookie Caleb Wilson with a broken right hand last week, the team announced that they would now be without the services of their valued big-named free agent acquisition from the offseason in veteran Norman Powell.</p><p>The guard tweaked his right hamstring at some point during the loss to the Wizards on Friday, and after having an MRI done it was determined that he would be shut down for the time being. The good news was that it was deemed mild and would be re-evaluated later this week. The bad news? Coach Tiago Splitter was now without his two leading scorers (Powell was 20.8 points per game and Wilson was 18.9).</p><p>“You know, next guy up,” Splitter said. “I don’t think it’s a new thing in the NBA, you gotta be ready for those moments. A lot of guys gotta step up, some of the guys that weren’t playing as many minutes are going to play more, and you go from there.”</p><p>True, but they also go on without one of their most experienced players, almost losing another coach on the floor.</p><p>Powell and Buddy Hield – both 33 – are the only 30-plus players on the roster, but what Powell brings is a resume filled with almost any scenario a player could go through in the NBA. From second-round pick in 2015, to fighting his way up through the G League, to NBA champion, and then last season, first-time All-Star, there’s few experiences that Powell hasn’t had to deal with.</p><p>That’s tough to duplicate in a young rebuild and a big reason the Bulls wrote the free-agent check for two years and $45 million. Next year, however, is a team option.</p><p>“Norm has been great,” Splitter said of Powell’s presence. “Just helping teammates, the coaching staff, his knowledge of the game, his experience of being in the NBA Finals. You add value when you have a guy like that in the locker room, around the players. We’re going to miss him on the court but he’s going to keep helping us in the locker room and stuff like that.”</p><p>With Powell sidelined, Hield got the starting nod against the Nuggets.</p><p></p><p><b>No joke</b></p><p></p><p>Splitter knows all about accomplished NBA big men, playing alongside Tim Duncan for several Spurs title runs.</p><p>So when discussing coaching against Nikola Jokic and just how special the perennial NBA MVP is, his take comes from experience.</p><p>“Unbelievable player,” Splitter said. “One of the most talented bigs that we’ve ever seen. The way he shoots the ball, his touch with the basketball is unbelievable. How he plays with one hand in the air, passes the ball, he sees everything. The strength and the IQ, very different player, so I’m a big fan.”</p><p></p><p><b>Speed kills</b></p><p></p><p>There’s a reason Splitter and his staff are trying to keep the minutes for back-up guard Tre Jones near the 20-minute mark per game.</p><p>In their estimation, Jones plays with so much speed and thrust that the best way to keep him effective is to keep him fresh.</p><p>“He brings a different spark, a different pace of basketball,” the coach said. “He pushes the pace with the ball in his hands. He touches the paint at will, makes defenses shrink, finds teammates, takes care of the ball, but of course he cannot play that many minutes.</p><p>“There’s a limit there with how fast can you play for that long? So I’ve got to be careful with his minutes because when he goes too far, he doesn’t play as fast, doesn’t play as sharp, so there’s a balance. We understand that.”</p>

entries.title: Bears offense didn't make a leap, even if their TE did
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ offense didn’t make a leap in Sunday’s 21-13 win against the Saints — but tight end Colston Loveland did.</p><p>On second down midway through the second quarter, the Bears’ tight end caught a pass in the right flat and hurdled safety Julian Blackmon at the 10. He landed in stride and streaked up the right sideline into Solider Field’s south end zone to a chorus of gasps, from his teammates and otherwise.</p><p>“I had my hands on my head,” tackle Theo Benedet said.</p><p>“That was mind-blowing,”  receiver Zavion Thomas said.</p><p>“He's super-athletic, isn't he?” coach Ben Johnson said.</p><p>Loveland had never hurdled a player on any level. His teammates had teased him for weeks, wondering whether he could jump.</p><p>“I’ve got to do it,” Loveland remember thinking. “I’ve got to try.”</p><p>In an alternate universe, Loveland’s touchdown would have sparked an outburst for quarterback Caleb Williams and the rest of the Bears’ offense. Instead, it was a rare flash of offensive excitement — the other being Thomas’ 40-yard pass from Williams on third-and-17 in the third quarter — in a game that left coach Ben Johnson and his quarterback shaking their heads.</p><p>“Putting up how many points we put up today with how the defense played …” Williams said. “No, not satisfied.”</p><p>Sunday was an improvement over Williams' last outing, a four-interception performance in a game the Bears were lucky to win against the Bucs. But it wasn’t quite the leap he was expecting, either.</p><p>The Bears started three possessions in Saints territory. They scored touchdowns on two — Loveland’s hurdle and a three-yard shovel pass to D’Andre Swift — and took a knee on the third. They started drives in their own territory eight times, and came away with two field goals, a fumble, an interception, a turnover on downs and three punts.</p><p>“I think we can be a lot better,” Williams said. “I think there was an opportunity for a lot of points out there.”</p><p>The Bears were favored by 11 ½ points, their largest margin since 2009. For the fifth-straight game, they won without ever trailing, the first time that’s happened to the franchise since 1959.</p><p>Still, Bears offensive players — and fans — left feeling unsatisfied.</p><p>“More,” Williams said. “That’s it.”</p><p>Call it the burden of championship expectations. The Bears won’t win one if their offense plays the way they did Sunday — even if they could beat the Saints. Williams went 15-for-23 for 181 yards, one interception — defensive end Chase Young batted a pass at the line of scrimmage that was picked Danny Stutsman late in the second quarter — and a 100.1 passer rating. Johnson’s evaluation of Williams was far from ebullient, though, sticking mostly with a stock I’m-going-to-have-to-watch-the-film response.</p><p>The Bears’ rushing attack averaged 4.4 yards per carry — above their 4.2-yard average — but was far from the dangerous weapon Johnson had hoped it would become after a few bye-week tweaks. And the Bears’ leading rusher, D’Andre Swift, fumbled in the fourth quarter.</p><p>“You want to win, and you want to win with style points,” Benedet said. “That’s the standard we have. I think it’s good to see the fans hold us to that standard too. That’s the culture we’re trying to build.”</p><p>The Bears say Williams is at his best when the lights are brightest. Sunday, the lights might have been more dim than at any point this season, down to the gray skies that turned everything a pallid hue. In the minds of many, Sunday’s game against the 3-7 Saints was mere undercard to their Thanksgiving game in Detroit, which is followed by a home contest against the AFC stalwart Jaguars.</p><p>“Every game counts as one, but this one [Thursday], because it's a divisional one, you could say it's one-and-a-half,” said Johnson, who is 0-2 in his head coaching career against his former team. “It's a big one, but we keep saying it every week — it's the next one. The next one's the biggest one.”</p><p>The Lions are in first place in the NFC North. The Bears are 0-2 in division play this year.</p><p>“There’s nowhere else we’d rather be, no division we’d rather be,” Loveland said. “We play the best. On Thanksgiving? That makes it even better.”</p><p>The Bears would have felt more comfortable had Sunday served as an offensive springboard. It wasn’t.</p><p>Williams rattled off what the offense needed to improve before Thursday’s game at Ford Field: harnessing energy and momentum and building successful plays off of each other.</p><p>“It's a big game for us,” Williams said. “We've got to go out there, we've got to execute, we've got to do all the things that good teams do.”</p>

entries.title: Bears notebook: Rookie WR Zavion Thomas back on Ben Johnson's good side, but D'Andre Swift? Not so much
entries.summary: <p>Rookie wide receiver <b>Zavion Thomas</b> is out of coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/20/bears-coach-ben-johnsons-straight-talk-changes-the-conversation-at-halas-hall" ><b>Ben Johnson</b></a>’s doghouse and veteran running back <b>D’Andre Swift</b> is back in it after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ 21-13 win over the Saints.</p><p>Thomas was benched offensively in the last game after committing a personal foul that cost the Bears a prime scoring chance against the Buccaneers but rebounded Sunday with a 30-yard run and two catches for 56 yards for the best game of his young career.</p><p>“I’ve always got to make plays,” Thomas said. “That’s what I’m brought here to do.”</p><p>Quarterback <b>Caleb Williams</b> was Thomas’ best friend. He flipped the field by hitting him on a 40-yard pass in the third quarter and threw a block for him on his long run in the second.</p><p>The Bears ran a reverse in which Williams pitched back to Swift, then Swift pitched to Thomas running to the left. Thomas had open space ahead thanks to downfield blocks by wide receiver <b>Rome Odunze</b> and right tackle <b>Theo Benedet</b>, and just needed a little help from Williams to get through the line of scrimmage.</p><p>Williams, flanking Thomas to his right, put his right shoulder into Saints 6-4, 273-pound defensive tackle <b>Colby Wooden</b> to buy Thomas just enough time.</p><p>“I knew he was going to go out there and get a block for me,” he said. “That’s pretty impressive.”</p><p>Johnson said Thomas is more “on it” when it comes to knowing the playbook, and his role will “continue to grow.”</p><p>Swift, meanwhile, lost his third fumble of the season and cost the Bears a chance to put the game away. Right after Montez Sweat’s safety early in the fourth quarter to put the Bears ahead 21-10, they had the ball in Saints’ territory when Swift coughed it up.</p><p>When asked if he said anything to Swift, who spent the rest of the game on the bench and finished with 51 yards on 13 rushes, Johnson said only, “Nope.”</p><p><b>Santos’ miss</b><br>Bears kicker <b>Cairo Santos</b> missed his first extra point since 2024, sending his kick in the second quarter wide right.</p><p>He went 2-for-2 on field goals, though, hitting from 41 yards on the opening possession and 35 yards in the third quarter.</p><p><b>Modest Monangai</b><br>In his return from the toe injury he suffered Oct. 4, running back <b>Kyle Monangai</b> managed just 18 yards on eight carries. The Bears turned to practice-squad back <b>Salvon Ahmed</b>, too, and he rushed six times for 33 yards.</p><p><b>Notes:</b><br>-- Linebacker <b>D’Marco Jackson</b>, center <b>Garrett Bradbury</b> and Benedet each got hurt during the game but returned. <br>-- Special teamer <b>Roschon Johnson</b> went to the locker room with an ankle injury early in the game.<br>-- Hall of Famer <b>Candace Parker</b>, a Naperville native who won a championship with the Chicago Sky, was at the game in a Bears hoodie.</p>

entries.title: Roman Kantserov powers Blackhawks to another victory during easier stretch
entries.summary: <p>VANCOUVER, British Columbia — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' lighter schedule has worked wonders on their mood and results.</p><p>The Hawks are suddenly 4-1-1 in their last six games after a 6-3 win Sunday against the last-place Canucks, following victories over the Sabres, Maple Leafs and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/21/blackhawks-flames-sam-rinzel-wyatt-kaiser-martin-pospisil" >Flames</a>. And in less than 48 hours, their season total of road wins increased from zero to two.</p><p>"We’re going to go through ups and downs, for sure, but we’ve got to just keep grinding and getting better every day," coach Jeff Blashill said. "If we do that with this group, I think the ceiling can grow because of how young we are."</p><p>Roman Kantserov earned his first hat trick Sunday with three goals from a cumulative 31 feet away from the net. </p><p>He continues to prove more and more convincingly that he'll be an elite goal-scorer in this league, even if very few of those goals are going to be pretty highlights.</p><p>"Maybe [in] my past years, I can shoot and score outside the net, but now I need to be in the slot," Kantserov said. "It's my job. I'm a forward. I need to be close to the net and make rebounds, make tips, score into the low pockets."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">GOAL: Roman Kantserov puts in a rebound for his first NHL hat trick. Wow. <a href="https://t.co/qYj4Iksnq1">pic.twitter.com/qYj4Iksnq1</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2124707427098427459?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 23, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>His 13 goals not only lead NHL rookies but also put him in a tie for 11th among all NHL players — level with the likes of Connor McDavid and Sebastian Aho. Two of his three Sunday came on the power play, but it's worth noting his nine goals during five-on-five play are tied for sixth-most league-wide.</p><p>"This is what I definitely saw on tape [from Russia]," Blashill said. "The only concern I had really was pace, because you don’t know the pace of the league. But since he’s been here, his pace has been good. He’s really good around the net...[and] knows how to score a lot of different ways. He’s a gifted goal-scorer, that’s for sure."</p><p>The Hawks raced out to a 4-0 lead after 13 minutes, survived the Canucks' voracious pushback through the middle of the game and did a decent job closing things out in the third period. That was enough to give backup goalie Drew Commesso (22 saves) a win in his first start this season.</p><p>The Hawks are now 1-11-1 against teams in the upper half of the current Stanley Cup odds yet 7-3-1 against teams in the lower half, WGN Radio's Charlie Roumeliotis pointed out. They've fared well against peers, but haven't learned how to punch above their weight.</p><p>Kevin Korchinski was a dark spot Sunday, making his first appearance since Nov. 7. Somehow in less than six minutes of ice time, he managed to take a penalty and be the man primarily responsible for two Canucks goals.</p><p>"Things didn’t go his way," said Blashill, who sounded more sympathetic than usual toward the much-debated young defenseman.</p>

entries.title: Coach Tiago Splitter making sure Bulls culture built on accountability
entries.summary: <p>Some messages are delivered with a soft pat on the back and a “we’ll get ‘em next time.” Others come courtesy of a sledgehammer.</p><p>That’s the fine line coach Tiago Splitter has been trying to walk with this Bulls roster through the first 16 games of the regular season.</p><p>A line that gets blurry at times.</p><p>Both Matas Buzelis and Josh Giddey are no strangers to seeing playing time come to an end for a seat on the bench when the play has gotten sloppy from them this season. Giddey even said of his benching in Cleveland last week that he would have “done the same thing if I was Tiago.”</p><p>However, it happened again in Friday’s loss to Washington in which Giddey and Buzelis played less than four minutes in the final quarter and according to a source, this time neither player was thrilled with the decision or felt it was warranted initially, especially Giddey.</p><p>Both players were given a better explanation on Saturday, calming the rough waters, and both Splitter and Giddey confirmed that even with Sunday’s 151-145 overtime loss to Denver at the United Center.</p><p>“He was really good about it,” Giddey said of the talk. “He doesn’t sugarcoat it, he tells you what you need to hear, not what you want to hear. As players it’s frustrating at the moment, you want to be out there to help your team win games. He hit it on the head the next day. Looking back at it now, it’s probably the things I needed to hear.”</p><p>Tough love from the first-year Bulls coach? Of course, but also further evidence that the front office wants this rebuild done right and that means establishing a culture of accountability. So if it feels like a Code Red being ordered from above, so be it.</p><p>“I think it’s simple: I’m trying to win the basketball game, trying to be competitive, and sometimes guys don’t have it,” Splitter said. “You try and put guys in there that you see are having a better day and go from there.”</p><p>Any surprise Splitter has this old school mentality? Not at all coming from Spurs culture and former coach Gregg Popovich.</p><p>What he won’t allow to happen is a young player run without a leash and play however he wants to. Whether that’s Buzelis, Giddey or rookie Caleb Wilson, who was benched in New York for bad body language.</p><p>“I don’t think it’s healthy, honestly, just to leave a guy there, playing 40 minutes and no accountability for anything,” Splitter said. “I don’t think that’s healthy. Yes, he’s going to have more experience, he’s going to have more shots, but is he playing the right way, is he playing the way we want? Sometimes not, and those reps are also bad reps. I want good reps. I think that’s how a player develops better.”</p><p>The on-the-court response from Giddey and Buzelis against the Nuggets? Message heard, as Giddey was spectacular in a triple-double showcase in which he scored 23 points, handed out a career-high 22 assists and grabbed 14 rebounds.</p><p>Buzelis was also solid, scoring 21 points and adding in two blocks.</p><p>The problem was the Bulls (4-12) had no answer for Nikola Jokic – few teams do – as the Denver star also recorded a triple-double, putting in 37 points, grabbing 18 rebounds and handing out 11 assists, while Jamal Murray led all scorers with 45 points.</p><p>Buzelis and Giddey were in for crunchtime.</p><p>“I talk to them, I explain, ‘This is why, this is how, and this is what I expect from you guys,’ “ Splitter added. “It’s not personal. Talking about Matas and Josh, great kids, great guys, they understand. They want to compete, they want to do right, they want to do well, and we know that. That’s not a question. You just have to do it more consistently and that’s fine, you’re going to learn from it.”</p>

entries.title: WATCH: Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen does the 'Stanky Legg'
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defensive coordinator Dennis Allen celebrated Sunday's win against his former team the way coach Ben Johnson usually does: by doing the "Stanky Legg."</p><p>Before Johnson led the Bears in their "Good, Better, Best" cheer after Sunday's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/22/bears-dt-jeffery-simmons-embraces-the-moment-with-3-sacks-in-a-21-13-win-over-saints" target="_blank" >21-13 win</a>, he introduced Allen. The Bears' defensive coordinator was the Saints' head coach from 2022-24 and an assistant there from 2006-10 and 2015-24. Allen walked into the middle of the room and pretended to slap his right knee, making his lower leg wobble. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Come for Good, Better, Best, stay for the DA stanky leg 👀 <a href="https://t.co/afAOYSWmwA">pic.twitter.com/afAOYSWmwA</a></p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2124624696867975660?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 22, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p> <br>It wasn't as smooth as Johnson's usual routine, but the Bears were in no place to complain. Allen called a defense that shut down the Saints, sacked them six times. All three game balls went to defensive players — tackle Jeffery Simmons, end Montez Sweat and cornerback Clark Phillips.</p><p>The Bears have now beaten the Saints in consecutive years. Both times, Johnson made it a point to include Allen in postgame celebrations.</p>

entries.title: Lead detonation in Iowa delayed until Wednesday as environmental groups say legal status remains uncertain
entries.summary: <p>A Sierra Club attorney said Sunday it remains unclear whether a court order temporarily putting on hold the Army’s EPA permit would prevent the Army from detonating nearly five tons of lead azide this week at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.</p><p>The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals issued an administrative stay of the EPA’s emergency permit Thursday, pending its ruling on the groups’ emergency motion. That prompted the federal government to say it would use its emergency authority to continue with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/11/20/the-army-plans-to-detonate-a-toxic-lead-compound-near-the-illinois-iowa-border-heres-what-to-know" >its plan to destroy the chemicals</a> being stored south of the Quad-Cities and near the Mississippi River.</p><p>The detonation is set to take place Wednesday for optimal weather conditions, the Army said in a post on X. The Army had originally planned to detonate the material Friday, then announced a delay until Monday before pushing it to Wednesday.</p><p>In a notice filed late Saturday, the U.S. Justice Department said the Army intends to invoke a separate emergency exclusion under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) to detonate the material without a permit from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency EPA permit no later than Nov. 24.</p><p>The federal government argues the court’s administrative stay of the EPA permit does not prevent the Army from acting under a separate RCRA emergency exclusion. The government said colder weather and continued delays could increase the danger.</p><p>Wally Taylor, legal chair for the Sierra Club’s Iowa Chapter, said the groups fighting to halt the detonation believe the court’s stay should stop the demolition, while the Army argues the order does not apply to action under the separate authority its invoking.</p><p>“I guess a lawyer’s answer is we don’t know.  It's a little up in the air,” Taylor said.</p><p>The Sierra Club is still asking the court to extend the stay, he said, though he is not confident the court can prevent the Army from acting.</p><p>" It's been really discouraging that the Army has not been more transparent about what they're doing and when they let people know," Taylor said. "We didn't know about this until just a few days ago, and the Army apparently has known about this for quite some time, but they haven't been very good about notifying the public."</p><p>He said his group and others want the demolition to be done safely and be followed by adequate cleanup if it proceeds.</p><p>The environmental groups said in a Sunday statement that declarations filed with the court challenged the Army’s public notice and questioned whether it had properly considered alternatives.</p><p>The groups have urged consideration of chemical neutralization, though the Army says that option would require prolonged handling of the 68 drums and increase the risk of an accidental explosion, the AP reported.</p><p>Cody Smith, program director at the Iowa Environmental Council, said the council had not received updated plume maps or modeling and was urging the Army to release them.</p><p> "We are less than 48 hours from their planned date of detonation according to the filing today, and we have yet to see any of that information," Smith said. "It's critical for Iowans and community leaders at every level to be able to protect themselves and their families from lead exposure, of which we know there is no safe level for humans."</p><p>Smith said the filings led the environmental council to believe detonation may now be the best treatment option, but he blamed the Army’s handling and storage of the material for creating the crisis.</p><p>He said the Army had not directly confirmed a date or time. Although the filings indicate a plan to act by Tuesday, he said the timing remained unconfirmed.</p><p>" I think it's really important that folks continue to call on the Army and on federal officials for transparency as soon as possible," Smith said. "If folks are looking for something to do, reaching out to their elected federal officials is probably the most helpful at this point."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/11/20/the-army-plans-to-detonate-a-toxic-lead-compound-near-the-illinois-iowa-border-heres-what-to-know" >The Army plans to detonate a toxic lead compound near the Illinois-Iowa border. Here’s what to know.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Guest's Thanksgiving dish tends to have dog hair in it
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I host Thanksgiving for our family and friends every year. All of our guests like to bring a dish to share. My problem is that one of my guests always makes a terrible dish: creamed onions. She brings two huge pans, and no one eats them. The main reason is the taste, but also because someone will find dog hair in it. Every. Single. Year. So now we all feel as if she is not preparing the food in a hygienic way and won't touch anything she brings.</p><p>After the meal, we allow everyone to fill to-go containers. The creamed onions go untouched. She always asks me to keep them, but I insist she take it home (because I'd throw it in the trash the moment she left, and I really hate to waste).</p><p>Is there a polite way to approach her about this? I don't want to hurt her feelings. If she really wants to contribute meaningfully to the meal, it would be best for her to bring something store-bought. This year, she has a new baby and is completely overwhelmed. Could I suggest that she go the store-bought route or that she bring nothing at all? — <i>THANKS, BUT NO THANKS</i></p><p><b>DEAR NO THANKS:</b> It's possible that this guest always brings her signature dish because she likes it, and her Thanksgiving wouldn't feel complete without it. Whatever the reason, there's no need to dissuade her or risk hurting her feelings. It sounds like everyone else has already learned to be wary of her cooking, so it can't cause any further harm.</p><p>To avoid the waste, you might tell her one pan is enough, considering how much you have had to send home with her in the past. Alternatively, you could frame it as "special dispensation": Tell her she's excused from bringing a dish if the baby is running her ragged.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> When an old friend was visiting from out of town, she made some observations about how my husband and I interact with each other and our children. Something she repeatedly commented on was that instead of shouting in our house, we text one another — not full conversations, but simple things like, "Honey, come to the living room," or "Son, bring the laundry up." She implied that it was disrespectful for our kids to summon me and my husband the same way. ("Daddy, can you come to the kitchen, please?") It doesn't bother us. We prefer it to running, shouting and searching through the house.</p><p>I chuckled and brushed off her comments, but I'd like your opinion on the topic. Do you think I need a comeback to her remarks? — <i>DIGITAL DAD IN ST. LOUIS</i></p><p><b>DEAR DAD:</b> If this is a common practice in your household, then I don't agree with your friend that it's disrespectful. In fact, I think it's even better than using an intercom as some wealthy families used to do. As for preparing a comeback to her giving her opinion, there's no need. You handled it appropriately. Let it rest.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i> </p>

entries.title: Stop Army's lead detonation at Illinois-Iowa border until all, including incarcerated, safeguarded
entries.summary: <p>Public outcry recently forced the U.S. Army to <a class="Link" href="https://www.kwqc.com/2026/11/20/middletown-detonation-postponed-acting-army-secretary-says/" target="_blank" ><u>postpone its plan</u></a> to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/11/20/the-army-plans-to-detonate-a-toxic-lead-compound-near-the-illinois-iowa-border-heres-what-to-know" >detonate</a> nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide at its ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, which is about 80 miles southwest of the Quad Cities. Residents demanded answers. Environmental groups went to court. Gov. JB Pritzker and <a class="Link" href="https://www.kwqc.com/2026/11/19/bipartisan-group-illinois-iowa-lawmakers-call-us-army-epa-consider-delaying-planned-detonation-lead-azide/" target="_blank" ><u>bipartisan elected officials demanded a delay</u></a>, citing toxic lead dust and inadequate notice and monitoring.</p><p>They were right. The Army initially postponed the detonation until Monday, three days before Thanksgiving. A federal appeals court has since temporarily suspended the Environmental Protection Agency permit while it considers a legal challenge brought by environmental groups. But the Army could still proceed, risking an environmental and public health disaster whose consequences could last for generations.</p><p>Families in Iowa and Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/resource-center/news/2026/november/18-release-2.html" target="_blank" ><u>have been told</u></a> that, depending on where the wind carries airborne particles, they may need to remain indoors for 24 to 48 hours with windows closed and outdoor air intake limited. Imagine preparing for Thanksgiving while wondering whether lead might settle on the yard or farmland. Who will test the soil? When will the results be public? What happens when the shelter-in-place advisory ends?</p><p>Amid the justified alarm over the safety of surrounding communities, another question demands attention: What protections are in place for the people living and working in nearby prisons, jails and detention centers?</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7d0000" name="module-7d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Just a few miles from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, people incarcerated at the <a class="Link" href="https://www.desmoinescounty.iowa.gov/sheriff/jail/" target="_blank" ><u>Des Moines County Jail in Burlington</u></a> have no ability to evacuate or control the air entering their cells. Iowa operates state prisons in Fort Madison and Mount Pleasant. In nearby Montrose, Iowa, the South Iowa Area Detention Service Agency operates a juvenile detention center. Across the Mississippi River are Illinois prisons and county jails, including Hill Correctional Center in Galesburg and East Moline Correctional Center near the Quad Cities. In Muscatine County, Iowa,<a class="Link" href="https://iowacapitaldispatch.com/2026/02/20/muscatine-countys-agreement-to-jail-ice-detainees-remains-secret/" target="_blank" ><u> the jail also detains people for </u></a>U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Together, these institutions hold thousands of incarcerated and detained people and employ hundreds of staff whose health and safety must also be accounted for.</p><p>These institutions are spread in different directions from the plant. Not all fall within the currently projected plume. But what if the wind changes?</p><p>I spent the COVID-19 pandemic documenting what happened when a public health emergency reached prisons and jails. Americans were told to avoid crowds, isolate when sick and improve ventilation. People in custody often had no power to do any of those things. Authorities determined where they slept, worked, ate and breathed. We saw the consequences.</p><p>Lead exposure is not a contagious disease. But the failure of public health guidance to account for confinement is painfully familiar.</p><p>We also have direct evidence that ventilation is inadequate at prisons in the region. In a <a class="Link" href="https://www.thejha.org/facilities/hill-correctional-center" target="_blank" ><u>2025 survey at Hill Correctional Center</u></a>, 81% of incarcerated respondents said ventilation was inadequate, while independent monitors observed vents clogged with dust. <a class="Link" href="https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/publications/SD/1601629.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Iowa’s own Department of Corrections</u></a> described ventilation in housing units at Mount Pleasant Correctional Facility as "very poor," citing high humidity and longstanding problems with air conditioning and mold.</p><p>Those findings show us why telling people to stay inside is not enough. If contaminated outdoor air enters a prison housing unit, incarcerated people cannot install filtration, relocate to another building or decide to leave. Reducing outdoor air intake may create other health hazards in already poorly ventilated, crowded spaces. Shelter is only protective when the air inside is safe.</p><p>People who work in these institutions share many of those same risks. Officers, nurses, teachers and other staff breathe the same air and return home to families facing the same uncertainty.</p><p>The danger will not end when the plume passes. <a class="Link" href="https://www.epa.gov/lead/lead-soil" target="_blank" ><u>Lead is an element and does not biodegrade</u></a>. If harmful quantities settle on soil or surfaces and are not removed, they can create exposure risks long after the day of the explosion. Children are especially susceptible to the effects of lead on brain development. Animals and farmland also warrant protection. The extent of any contamination is unknown, making transparent sampling and enforceable cleanup essential.</p><p>The Army says the explosives have become too unstable to move safely. That danger must be taken seriously. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.epa.gov/ia/iowa-army-ammunition-plant-middletown-iowa-3" target="_blank" ><u>EPA has issued an emergency permit</u></a> requiring environmental sampling, monitoring and cleanup. But a permit is not proof that every community, institution or family has been adequately protected.</p><h3>Protection and accountability </h3><p>In their <a class="Link" href="https://www.kwqc.com/2026/11/19/bipartisan-group-illinois-iowa-lawmakers-call-us-army-epa-consider-delaying-planned-detonation-lead-azide" target="_blank" ><u>Nov 19 letter</u></a>, Pritzker and seven other elected officials demanded answers about the plume under changing weather conditions, safer alternatives and monitoring before and after detonation. Those demands should extend explicitly to every prison, county jail, juvenile detention center and immigration detention site that could be affected. Have those facilities been included in alternative wind scenarios? Have their ventilation systems been evaluated? Are staff and people in custody being informed? Who will test their air, soil and surfaces, and who will ensure medical follow-up if exposure occurs?</p><p>During the pandemic, families struggled to learn whether incarcerated loved ones were sick, receiving care or even alive. No family should face that uncertainty again.</p><p>The public raised the alarm. Elected officials responded. The Army delayed the explosion. Now that pressure must produce more than a new date: officials must demonstrate protection and accountability for contamination if it occurs.</p><p>The Army's postponement has not diminished the enormity of what is at stake. The potential consequences extend far beyond the day of the explosion. Lead deposited in soil can remain for generations, threatening children, families, wildlife, farmland and the communities that depend on them. The people living and working in nearby prisons, jails and detention centers are part of those communities, and their safety cannot be an afterthought. </p><p>Before proceeding, the Army must demonstrate that it can protect everyone potentially affected — including people who live and work inside of Iowa and Illinois’ jails and prisons. If it cannot, the detonation must not go forward.</p><p><i>Amanda Klonsky is a researcher and writer based in Chicago. Her work focuses on incarceration, public health, education and racial equity.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2e0000" name="module-2e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Can the Soul Train Awards help boost Chicago’s reputation as an entertainment destination?
entries.summary: <p>Chicago rolled out a purple carpet for Chaka Khan, Common, Durand Bernarr, Lucky Daye and a host of other celebrities at BET’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/11/05/soul-train-awards-queen-latifah-durand-bernarr-chicago-bet" target="_blank" ><u>Soul Train Awards</u></a>, which taped earlier this month at the Harris Theater for Music and Dance for a special that airs Friday at 7 p.m. on BET and CBS.</p><p>The excitement was palpable as they mingled with attendees dressed in their best sparkly suits, golden gowns and festive hats.</p><p>“You can feel it in the atmosphere,” said food influencer Keith Lee, who was among the high-profile guests and plans to host a culinary festival in the city next fall. “It's the culture. It's the people. Soul is what brings us together.”</p><p>The spin-off awards show is making a comeback after a two-year hiatus, and it’s a big test for both the “Soul Train” brand and Chicago, where the long-running TV program originated. ><u>cultural phenomenon</u></a> that originated locally on WCIU-TV, and ran nationally in syndication from 1971 to 2006. It exposed millions to the best of Black music, fashion and dance, including the now-iconic “Soul Train line” that is now emulated by another Chicago native, Jennifer Hudson, on her talk show. Everyone from The Jackson 5 and Gladys Knight and The Pips to LL Cool J and Usher<b> </b>graced the stage.</p><p>As a host, Cornelius has been described as the “epitome of cool,” known for his style and catchphrases, such as “Love, peace and soul.” His goal was to counteract negative media narratives by showing Black people in “a more positive light,” said his son Tony Cornelius, who now lives in Los Angeles.</p><p>“Soul Train was a gift that he wanted to give back to our people,” said Tony, who grew up on the South Side and worked alongside his father as a producer on the show.</p><div entries.title: As the Trump administration puts ankle monitors on more immigrants, it’s taking over this Chicagoan’s life
entries.summary: <p>Lately, Liz has been jolted awake at night in a panic when her ankle monitor starts to vibrate. The buzzing reminds her of her greatest fear: that immigration agents will barge into her small apartment on Chicago’s North Side and take her away to a detention center.</p><p>“ICE agents told me the monitor would vibrate if it’s broken or tampered with,” she says crying. “ ‘We’ll look for you right away,’ ” she says they told her, “ ‘because we know where to find you.’ ”</p><p>The Guatemalan asylum-seeker has been living in a constant state of anxiety since she, her husband and daughter were asked to show up for an unexpected immigration check-in last August. Her husband was taken into immigration custody while Liz was fitted with an ankle monitor and released with her 15-year-old daughter. Neither she nor her husband have criminal records.</p><p>WBEZ is not using their full names because they fear government retaliation.</p><p>“I asked the immigration agents, ‘Why? Did we do something wrong?’ ” Liz says in her native Spanish, adding that since the family arrived in the United States in 2024 from Guatemala they’ve been trying to follow every step of their asylum application process by the book.</p><p>Like Liz, more than 53,000 noncitizens nationwide in 2026 have been fitted with ankle monitors under the Department of Homeland Security’s Alternatives to Detention program, according to government data. That number has more than tripled since 2024 as the Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement. It’s the same trend locally, a WBEZ/Sun-Times analysis found. So far this year, ICE’s Chicago field office — which oversees Illinois, Indiana, Wisconsin, Missouri, Kentucky, and Kansas — has issued nearly 3,800 ankle monitors — a nearly 40% jump since 2024.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-950000" name="html-embed-module-950000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30950504"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30950504/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The surge has raised concerns among immigration advocates over the mental health toll they say the constant surveillance takes on those who wear the ankle device and pose no risk. Advocates argue the use of ankle monitors was supposed to be an alternative to detention but as more people have been fitted with them, detentions have also increased.</p><p>“We have seen so many people across the country who have been complying with their immigration cases, who have families, who have jobs, who have strong community ties, no significant criminal history, going to their regular appointments and suddenly getting shackled with ankle monitoring,” says Lauren Hodges, senior attorney with Amica Center for Human Rights, a legal advocacy group.</p><p>Advocates like Hodges point out that the upward trend began soon after an internal Trump administration directive last year ordering immigration agents to fit noncitizens with ankle monitors “whenever possible.”</p><p>Her organization filed a <a class="Link" href="https://acrobat.adobe.com/id/urn:aaid:sc:US:4d60693e-0c67-40a7-85d7-6ed671007d97" target="_blank" ><u>class action lawsuit</u></a> that accuses the Trump administration of requiring noncitizens to wear an ankle or wrist monitor without providing justification for why such "harmful and invasive" monitoriing is warranted. The lawsuit says people fitted with the devices have experienced health problems as result, such as high blood pressure, as well as anxiety and depression.</p><p>The Department of Homeland Security did not answer specific questions about its increased use of ankle monitors or any other questions about this tracking device. In a statement, the agency defended the ATD program as a critical tool to ensure “compliance with release conditions, and regular check-ins.”</p><p>The agency says people without a flight risk or criminal history are enrolled because it is the most “cost-efficient way to ensure compliance with their immigration proceedings.”</p><p><b>Effects on mental health</b></p><p>Alternatives to Detention was started more than 20 years ago as a way to keep track of immigrants who were released under supervision while facing deportation.</p><p>But advocates say the continual surveillance is just a different form of detention.</p><p>When the Trump administration stripped Haitians of their Temporary Protected Status in June — which allowed hundreds of thousands of immigrants fleeing natural disasters or political conflict back home to live and work in the U.S. temporarily — many were later fitted with ankle monitors. Among them was Pierre Damas Bel, a college student and star soccer player. <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/02/nx-s1-5953998/remembering-pierre-damas-bel-an-ohio-college-student-with-great-promise" target="_blank" ><u>News reports say</u></a> he struggled deeply with the humiliation of the device, even sharing his frustrations on social media before taking his own life.</p><p>Liz and her family have also struggled with shame and anxiety around the device. At that August check-in, Liz says immigration officials openly debated putting an ankle monitor on her 15-year-old daughter, even though federal guidelines restrict ICE from placing tracking devices on minors.</p><p>Overhearing the agents, the high schooler, who plays flag football, began sobbing. She worried about being bullied at school or perceived as a criminal.</p><p>“When I saw her little face and she started crying, she said to me, ‘Mommy, I won’t be able to play anymore.’”</p><p>Agents ultimately let the teen go without one.</p><p>Since then, Liz says the shame of wearing an ankle monitor has been devastating. Strapped tightly to her leg, the device is bulky and uncomfortable.</p><p>“When I go to church, I like to wear a skirt or a dress, and now I can’t,” she says. “I have to wear a long dress so people don’t stare at me. It’s embarrassing.”</p><p>“We’re making the act of being an immigrant a criminal state,” says Jennifer Babaie, associate director of the Adult Detention Project at the National Immigrant Justice Center. “The majority of the people being arrested are folks that are applying or [are] otherwise in a legal status ... now you’re on an ankle monitor, and you’re suddenly in a completely different category. “</p><p>Not only are more people wearing ankle monitors, but they are wearing them for longer.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-150000" name="html-embed-module-150000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30965054"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30965054/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>ICE has increasingly imposed GPS ankle monitors on immigrants even after federal judges have ordered they be released from custody because the government has failed to justify the detention, Anthony Enriquez, vice president of U.S. advocacy and litigation at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, said during a recent <a class="Link" href="https://austinkocher.substack.com/p/this-is-really-an-alternative-form" target="_blank" ><u>panel</u></a> led by data journalist Austin Kocher.</p><p>Human rights advocates argue that the federal ankle monitor policy is not necessary and is driven by <a class="Link" href="https://acrobat.adobe.com/id/urn:aaid:sc:US:4d60693e-0c67-40a7-85d7-6ed671007d97" target="_blank" ><u>cruelty</u></a> and the profits the companies who supply the ankle monitors are making. The cost of the technology rose from roughly $25,500 per day in 2022 to more than $145,000 in 2026.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure She is currently studying English.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>Constant anxiety the monitor won’t work</b></p><p>Liz says her family has always been under some form of federal surveillance. Her husband was fitted with an ankle monitor when he first arrived in the United States in 2024. Still, the family managed to find work and build a life in Chicago after fleeing violence and street crime in Guatemala. He worked as a scrap metal collector, and she cleaned homes.</p><p>Now, Liz is trying to hold the family together on her own.</p><p>But she’s struggling.</p><p>In late October, Liz received an unexpected message ordering her to report for an immigration check-in at the same building where her husband was arrested. She worried agents would accuse her of tampering with her ankle monitor and take her into custody.</p><p>“I’m coming here prepared for anything, because I don’t know what could happen to me inside,” she says.</p><p>On the morning of her appointment, Liz’s attorney could not attend, so she arranged for a pro bono lawyer to accompany her. She says her 15-year-old daughter was crying as she walked out the door.</p><p>But this time that appointment went OK.</p><p>A technical glitch had caused her ankle monitor to stop sending location data to ICE, triggering the urgent check-in to verify she had not cut it off. Maybe this time, she got lucky, or bringing an attorney made a difference.</p><p>But that relief is temporary. The tracker — and the anxiety and fear it brings — isn't going anywhere.</p><p><i>Contributing: Keenan Chen</i></p>

entries.title: Chicago top cop finalist was suspended 3 times while racking up dozens of misconduct complaints
entries.summary: <p>Over his 27-year career with the Chicago Police Department, records show Counterterrorism Chief Christopher Papaioannou has racked up dozens of misconduct complaints and been suspended three times.</p><p>Now, Papaioannou wants to run the department.</p><p>He was named this month as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/12/chicago-police-superintendent-search-finalists-ursitti-novalez-papaioannou" >one of the three finalists</a> to become the next superintendent, along with First Deputy Supt. Antoinette Ursitti and Community Policing Chief Angel Novalez. But Papaioannou's bid could be dogged by his disciplinary record, which includes 33 complaints, according to records obtained from the Chicago Police Department and the city's Civilian Office of Police Accountability.</p><p>His suspensions in three sustained cases, totaling 15 days, came after investigators found he carried out a wrongful raid, pepper-sprayed a crowd at a drag-racing event and failed to report that he'd tackled a crime suspect, the records show. He has also been named in lawsuits that have cost the city $160,000.</p><p>By comparison, Novalez has been the subject of 10 complaints, one of which led to a recommended two-day suspension for failing to report another officer's misconduct. None of the eight complaints naming Ursitti has been sustained, records show.</p><p>The Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability, the body that led the superintendent search, said it "reviewed each candidate’s disciplinary history, with particular attention to the cases in which complaints were sustained."</p><p>"We discussed those matters directly with the candidates and gave them the opportunity to address our questions," the commission said in a statement. "The Commission is confident that all three finalists have the knowledge, experience, judgment, and character necessary to serve as strong leaders of the Chicago Police Department.”</p><p>But when the commission voted earlier this month on the three finalists to replace retired Supt. Larry Snelling, commissioner Angelique Guzman opposed Papaioannou’s nomination.</p><p>In an interview, Guzman said Papaioannou’s misconduct record and background in SWAT weighed heavily on her decision to vote "no." She felt he didn't take full accountability when questioned about a sustained complaint stemming from a summer 2020 protest.</p><p>“I really just did not think that right now in this current time, with the whole year that we had to face because of Midway Blitz and people, community members feeling unsafe in their own homes and their neighborhoods, that we needed a superintendent like Papaioannou,” Guzman said. “We need a superintendent that actually is willing to make sure that CPD is held accountable and actually progress in the consent decree.”</p><p>Papaioannou has allegedly expressed disdain toward the disciplinary system, according to a complaint filed in August saying he called a sergeant an ableist slur.</p><p>“I don’t give a f--- about [complaints],” Papaioannou allegedly told officers. “Add his comment to my pile of them.”</p><p>He and the other candidates didn’t respond to requests for comment. Neither did the mayor's office.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cf0000" Novalez.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>A series of suspensions</b></h3><p>Papaioannou oversaw the wrongful raid of a home in Englewood in April 2006, when he was an officer<b>.</b></p><p>He and other officers forced their way into a home not listed on a search warrant and ordered residents to the ground at gunpoint, according to a lawsuit. A 2-year-old and 11-year-old were among those inside the home.</p><p>Papaioannou and the other cops ordered the 11-year-old to place herself in handcuffs at gunpoint, the lawsuit alleged.</p><p>The residents eventually told the cops they were in the wrong house after being shown a copy of the search warrant Papaioannou had obtained, according to the lawsuit. Officers then told the residents to “shut up” and continued the search.</p><p>The department gave Papaioannou a one-day suspension, and the city was ordered to pay $100,000 to the residents.</p><p>In May 2020, when Papaioannou was a commander, he failed to properly document a use-of-force incident during a protest against the police killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis.</p><p>During a gathering in Lincoln Park, a person jumped onto a vehicle and began chanting, then refused to get down when ordered by police, according to disciplinary records. When officers approached, the person took off and Papaioannou conducted an emergency takedown, records show.</p><p>COPA found the use of force to be justified, but Papaioannou admittedly failed to report the incident to the department.</p><p>The oversight agency recommended a seven-day suspension for the recording error. Then-Supt. David Brown disagreed with the findings, but the Chicago Police Board upheld COPA’s recommendation.</p><p>Papaioannou’s final sustained complaint stemmed from his response to a drag-racing incident in August 2022, when he was a deputy chief.</p><p>COPA found Papaioannou discharged pepper spray into a group of people without justification, failed to report a firearm-pointing incident and didn’t properly supervise an officer who shattered a car window with a baton.</p><p>Snelling, then the superintendent, disagreed with the latter two findings and called for COPA to reduce its recommended 45-day suspension. Chicago police officials and the oversight agency met and agreed to a seven-day suspension. COPA acknowledged the “enormous stress” Papaioannou was under during the seven-hour incident, and his fear for the safety of himself and other officers.</p><p>Papaioannou's latest complaint was related to a roll call at Lollapalooza. Someone reported Papaioannou called a sergeant a slur for intellectually disabled people, then announced he didn’t care if they filed complaints against him.</p><p>Investigators later determined there wasn't enough information to proceed with that case, and it was administratively closed, records show.</p><p>Papaioannou has earned various awards and commendations from the department. And in 2021, he won the Law Enforcement Official of the Year Award from the Illinois Security Professionals Association. </p><p>The other two superintendent candidates<b> </b>have recently held high-ranking administrative roles and have received far fewer complaints during their careers, both of which have stretched 26 years.</p><p>Novalez’s only sustained complaint came after he failed to properly report an officer who released an impounded vehicle without authorization in June 2011. He was issued a two-day suspension, according to the disciplinary records.</p><p>The bulk of Ursitti’s eight complaints have centered around allegations of workplace discrimination lodged against her and other high-ranking police officials. The complainant filed a lawsuit in 2024, but it was later dismissed.</p><p>Alexandra Block is an attorney with the ACLU of Illinois, which is part of the coalition of community groups and civil rights organizations that negotiated a federal consent decree mandating sweeping reforms to the police department.</p><p>Block wouldn’t comment on specific candidates, but she emphasized the importance of Mayor Brandon Johnson selecting a superintendent who represents the best values of the department.</p><p>"We are hoping for a candidate who takes the consent decree very seriously and whose primary focus will be to transform the culture of CPD into an accountable professional organization that treats all members of the public in Chicago equitably and impartially,” she said. </p><div
